text: Motion with constant acceleration. Before using the constant acceleration equations, we need to decide whether this model applies. These equations are powerful, but they only describe motion where the acceleration is constant over the interval being analyzed. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. A car accelerates from rest, then later breaks to a stop. Should the entire trip be modeled with one constant acceleration, or should it be split into separate intervals? Choosing a one-dimensional motion model. Use the following questions before choosing an equation. Is the motion along one straight axis? If yes, the motion can be described with one-dimensional position, velocity, and acceleration. Is the acceleration constant over the interval? If yes, the constant acceleration equations can be used. If no, use graphs, calculus, or split the motion into intervals where the acceleration is approximately constant. Are the known and unknown quantities among x, x0, v, v0, a, and t? If yes, choose an equation that contains the unknown and the given quantities. Does the sign of the answer make physical sense? Check whether the object is moving in the expected direction, speeding up or slowing down appropriately, and whether any time value is physically meaningful. A Khan Academy video is linked on the course webpage. Notation. To make things simpler, we introduce some conventions in notation. One simplification is taking t0 equals 0, which is the point in time when you begin to measure. Time exists before this point, but until you get your delorean to 88 miles per hour, then it doesn't make sense to include the past. The elapsed time goes from delta t equals t final minus t0 to delta t equals t. We don't need the subscript f anymore. So the elapsed time is delta t equals t. We can drop the subscript f from the delta x and delta v as well. In our simplified notation, we have delta t equals t, delta x equals x minus x0, delta v equals v minus v0, where the subscript o denotes an initial value and the absence of a subscript indicates the final value of the variable. For now, we will also make the assumption that the acceleration is constant. As a result, the average and instantaneous acceleration are equal, or average acceleration equals a equals constant. In many situations in this course, the acceleration is constant. When it isn't, for example, a car accelerating to top speed than breaking to a stop, the motion will be considered in separate parts, like with the runner, and each part has its own constant acceleration. Displacement and position from velocity. To get our first two equations, we start with the definition of average velocity. The average velocity equals delta x over delta t, and substitute the simplified notation to get average velocity equals x minus x0 over t. Solving for x gives x equals x0 plus average velocity times t, where the arithmetic average velocity is average velocity equals the quantity v0 plus v divided by 2. This version of average velocity reflects that when acceleration is constant, then average velocity is the simple average of the initial and final velocities. Solving for final velocity from acceleration and time. We can derive another useful equation by manipulating the definition of acceleration, a equals delta v over delta t. By substituting the simplified notation for delta v and delta t, we have a equals the quantity v minus v0 divided by t for constant acceleration. Solving for v yields v equals v0 plus a t for constant acceleration. The above equation gives us insight into relationships among velocity, acceleration, and time. We can see that final velocity depends on both acceleration and time. For zero acceleration, then the initial and final velocities are equal, i.e. v equals v0. If a is less than zero, then v is less than v0. These relationships fit our intuition, which can be a good sign. Example problem, calculating final velocity. The problem. An airplane lands with an initial velocity of 70.0 meters per second, and then accelerates opposite to the motion at 1.50 meters per second squared for 40.0 seconds. What is its final velocity? The model. The airplane moves in one dimension with constant acceleration. We choose the initial direction of motion as positive. Since the acceleration is opposite the motion, the acceleration is negative in this coordinate system. The math. For constant acceleration, the final velocity is related to the initial velocity, acceleration, and elapsed time by v equals v0 plus a t. The acceleration is negative because it points opposite the positive direction of motion. So the velocity time relation gives v equals v0 plus a t equals 70.0 meters per second plus negative 1.50 meters per second squared times 40.0 seconds equals 10.0 meters per second. The conclusion. The airplane's final velocity is 10.0 meters per second. The result is still positive, so the airplane is still moving in its original direction after 40.0 seconds, but it has slowed substantially. The problem. Dragsters can achieve an average acceleration of 26.0 meters per second squared. Suppose a dragster accelerates from rest at this rate for 5.56 seconds. How far does it travel in this time? The model. The dragster is modeled as a particle moving in one dimension with constant acceleration. It starts from rest at the starting line, which we choose as the origin. With these choices, the displacement is determined by the acceleration and the elapsed time. The math. For one dimensional motion with constant acceleration, the position is given by x equals x0 plus v0 times t plus 1.5 a t squared. Because the dragster starts from rest at the origin, v0 equals 0 and x0 equals 0, so the position equation reduces to x equals 1.5 a t squared. The displacement after 5.56 seconds is found by evaluating this expression, which gives x equals 1.5 times 26.0 meters per second squared times 5.56 seconds squared equals 402 meters. The conclusion. The dragster travels 402 meters while accelerating from rest for 5.56 seconds. The large displacement over a short time is physically reasonable because the acceleration is very large. Use backslash left and backslash right whenever the expression contains fractions, roots, or stacked exponents. This keeps your math clean, readable, and professional, especially in physics derivations. Difference of squares identity. A very common algebra identity is A plus B times A minus B equals A squared minus B squared. You can see it by distributing or using foil to save a step. A plus B times A minus B equals A times A minus B plus B times A minus B equals A squared minus A B plus A B minus B squared equals A squared minus B squared. This is useful for quickly simplifying expressions and for factoring quadratics that look like a difference of squares. We can see the following relationships in this equation. Final velocity depends on the acceleration and total displacement. For a fixed acceleration, the stopping distance x minus x naught increases with the square of the velocity. It takes much farther to stop at a higher speed. This is shown by x minus x naught equals V naught squared divided by 2A, which is proportional to V naught squared. Example problem. Calculating final velocity. The problem. A dragster starts from rest and accelerates at an average rate of A equals 26.0 meters per second squared. In the previous example, it traveled a displacement of delta x equals x minus x naught equals 402 meters. Use a kinematic equation that does not involve time to find the dragster's final velocity. The model. The dragster moves in one dimension with constant acceleration. It starts from rest and moves in the positive direction. Since the elapsed time is not needed, we use the time independent relationship between speed, acceleration, and displacement. The math. For constant acceleration, the time independent kinematic equation is V squared equals V naught squared plus 2A times x minus x naught. Because the dragster starts from rest, V naught equals 0. And because the displacement is delta x equals x minus x naught, the time independent equation becomes V squared equals 2A times delta x. The final speed is the positive square root because the dragster accelerates forward, which gives V equals the square root of 2A times delta x equals the square root of 2 times 26.0 meters per second squared times 402 meters equals 145 meters per second. The conclusion. The dragster's final velocity is 145 meters per second in the forward direction. The positive root is selected because the dragster starts from rest and accelerates forward. Time-based form A equals the quantity V minus V naught divided by T. If the delta velocity V minus V naught is small and the time T is finite, the acceleration is small. If V equals V naught, then A equals 0. There is no acceleration. But if we try to change velocity by a finite amount in an extremely short time as T approaches 0, the acceleration becomes very large. This situation does not represent realistic motion. It corresponds to an instantaneous jump in velocity, which would require an infinite force. Displacement-based form A equals the quantity V squared minus V naught squared divided by 2 times the quantity x minus x naught. If the velocity change is small and the displacement is finite, the acceleration is small. If V equals V naught, the numerator is 0 and A equals 0. If a finite velocity change occurs over almost no distance, the acceleration again becomes very large. This describes another unphysical situation, a sharp change in motion over essentially zero distance. How calculus resolves the issue? When both the delta velocity and the time or displacement become small together, these expressions take the indeterminate form 0 over 0. In that limit, acceleration must be defined using a derivative. A equals the limit as delta T approaches 0 of delta V over delta T, which equals DV over DT. This definition ensures that acceleration remains finite for smooth, realistic motion. Key takeaway. Very large accelerations arise when velocity changes to abruptly. Real objects change velocity smoothly, not instantaneously. Calculus replaces finite differences with derivatives to correctly describe motion at an instant. This is why sharp corners on velocity graphs imply infinite acceleration and why real motion curves are smooth. Example problem. Calculating time. The problem. A car merges into freeway traffic on a straight 200 meter long on ramp. If its initial velocity is V0 equals 10.0 meters per second and it accelerates uniformly at A equals 2.00 meters per second squared, how long does it take the car to travel 200 meters up the ramp? The model. The car moves in one dimension with constant acceleration along the ramp. We choose the start of the ramp as the origin and take the direction of motion as positive. The known displacement, initial velocity and acceleration determine the travel time through the constant acceleration position equation. The math. For constant acceleration, the position is given by x equals x0 plus V0 times t plus 1 half a t squared with the start of the ramp as the origin x0 equals 0 and x equals 200 meters. So the position equation gives 200 meters equals 10.0 meters per second times t plus 1 half 2.00 meters per second squared times t squared. 0 equals t squared plus 10.0t minus 200. Applying the quadratic formula to the equation t squared plus 10.0t minus 200 equals 0 gives t equals negative 10.0 plus or minus the square root of 10.0 squared minus 4 times 1 times negative 200 all divided by 2 times 1 which equals negative 10.0 plus or minus 30.0 divided by 2. The two mathematical roots are t equals 10.0 seconds and t equals negative 20.0 seconds. The negative root corresponds to a time before the modeled motion begins, so the physical travel time is t equals 10.0 seconds. The conclusion. The car takes 10.0 seconds to travel the 200 meter on ramp. The negative mathematical root is rejected because it does not describe the time after the car begins the modeled motion. The problem. A spaceship has left Earth's orbit and is on its way to the moon. It accelerates at 20.0 meters per second squared for two minutes and covers a distance of 1000 kilometers. What are the initial and final velocities of the spaceship? The model. The spaceship moves in one dimension with constant acceleration. Both the initial and final velocities are unknown, so the displacement relation is used first to determine the initial velocity. The velocity time relation is then used to determine the final velocity. The math. For constant acceleration, the displacement is related to initial velocity, acceleration and time by x minus x0 equals v0 times t plus 1 half a t squared. It is convenient to work in kilometers for position and time for time. Converting the acceleration and elapsed time gives a equals 20.0 meters per second squared equals 0.0200 kilometers per second squared. t equals 2 minutes, which equals 120 seconds. Solving the displacement equation for the initial velocity gives v0 equals the quantity x minus x0 minus 1 half a t squared divided by t equals 1000 kilometers minus 1 half times 0.0200 kilometers per second squared times 120 seconds squared all divided by 120 seconds equals 7.13 kilometers per second. The final velocity is found from the velocity time relation, which gives v equals v0 plus a t equals 7.13 kilometers per second plus 0.0200 kilometers per second squared times 120 seconds equals 9.53 kilometers per second. The conclusion. The spaceship's initial velocity is 7.13 kilometers per second and its final velocity is 9.53 kilometers per second. The final velocity is larger because the spaceship accelerates in the direction of motion throughout the interval. The problem. A cheetah waits in hiding behind a bush. The cheetah spots a gazelle running past at 10 meters per second. At the instant the gazelle passes the cheetah, the cheetah accelerates from rest at 4.0 meters per second squared to catch the gazelle. Part A. How long does it take for the cheetah to catch the gazelle? Part B. What is the displacement of the gazelle and the cheetah? The model. This is a one-dimensional pursuit problem involving two objects. We choose the point where the gazelle passes the cheetah as the origin and take the direction of motion as positive. The gazelle moves with constant velocity while the cheetah starts from rest and accelerates uniformly. The cheetah catches the gazelle when both animals have the same position at the same time. The math. The gazelle moves with constant velocity so its position is x sub g equals v sub g t. The cheetah starts from rest with constant acceleration so its position is x sub c equals one half a sub c t squared. Part A. At the catch time the two positions are equal which gives x sub g equals x sub c. v sub g t equals one half a sub c t squared. The non-zero catch time is found by dividing both sides by t and solving for t which gives v sub g equals one half a sub c t. t equals two v sub g over a sub c equals two times ten meters per second divided by four point zero meters per second squared equals five point zero seconds. Part B. The catch displacement is found by evaluating the gazelle's position at t equals five point zero seconds which gives x sub g equals v sub g t equals ten meters per second times five seconds equals fifty meters. The cheetah's position gives the same displacement at the catch time which is x sub c equals one half a sub c t squared equals one half times four point zero meters per second squared times five point zero seconds squared equals fifty meters. The conclusion. The cheetah catches the gazelle after five point zero seconds. Both animals have traveled fifty meters from the starting point when the catch occurs.
